<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Condition~\textup{(TU)}{} is false. More precisely, there are real numbers
$\nu,\nu'\in(0,1)$ with $\nu$ irrational and $\nu'-\nu\in\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12]$ such that
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}f_N(\sqrt\nu)\ne\limsup_{N\to\infty}f_N(\sqrt{\nu'}).
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:lebesgue}
\textup{(TU)}{} does hold for Lebesgue-almost every $\nu$. By Borel's theorem and since
$\nu\mapsto\sqrt{\nu+d}$ maps null sets to null sets, for almost every $\nu$
the numbers $\sqrt{\nu+d}$ are simply normal for all $d\in\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12]$ at once. So
whether \textup{(TU)}{} holds ``almost everywhere'' depends on the reference measure,
and the second proof shows that this cannot be repaired by passing to a
measure-theoretic form of \textup{(TU)}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:tu}
\emph{Condition~\textup{(TU)}} is the statement: for all $\nu,\nu'\in(0,1)$ with $\nu$
irrational and the same tail, and for every strictly increasing sequence
$(n_i)$ of natural numbers,
\[
\limsup_{i\to\infty}f_{n_i}(\sqrt\nu)=\limsup_{i\to\infty}f_{n_i}(\sqrt{\nu'}).
\]
We write $\textup{(TU)}_1$ for the same statement with only $n_i=i$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:shift}
Let $a,b$ be real and $s,K\in\mathbb{N}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $X_{k+s}(a)=X_k(b)$ for all $k\ge K$, then $f_N(a)-f_N(b)\to0$.
\item If $X_{k+s}(a)=1-X_k(b)$ for all $k\ge K$, then $f_N(a)+f_N(b)\to1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
In both cases $|S_N(a)-S_N(b)|$, respectively $|S_N(a)+S_N(b)-N|$, is at most
$K+2s$ for every $N$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:carry}
Let $z,w$ be real and $m\ge1$ with $X_m(z)=0$ and
$\lfloor2^mz\rfloor\le\lfloor2^mw\rfloor\le\lfloor2^mz\rfloor+1$. Then
$\lfloor2^kw\rfloor=\lfloor2^kz\rfloor$ for all $k<m$; in particular $z$ and
$w$ have the same first $m-1$ digits. Consequently, if $X_n(z)=0$, then
$S_N(z+2^{-n})\le S_N(z)+1$ for all $N$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since $\lfloor2^mz\rfloor$ is even, the two values at level $m$ have the same
quotient by $2$, and one descends from $k$ to $k-1$ using
$\lfloor2^{k}t\rfloor=2\lfloor2^{k-1}t\rfloor+X_{k}(t)$. For the second
statement, $z+2^{-n}$ agrees with $z$ in the first $n-1$ digits, has digit $1$
at $n$, and agrees with $z$ after $n$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:zero}
Let $z$ be real and $M\ge1$. There is $m>M$ with $X_m(z)=0$ and
$f_{m-1}(z)\ge f_M(z)$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
No expansion of the form $X_k=1$ for all $k>M$ occurs with our digit
convention, so there is a first $m>M$ with $X_m(z)=0$. The digits between $M$
and $m$ are all $1$, so the frequency does not decrease from $M$ to $m-1$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:local}
Assume $\textup{(TU)}_1$. Let $y$ be irrational with $1/2<y<1$ and $y^2\in\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12]$. Then
$f_N(y)\ge2/5$ for infinitely many~$N$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Put $\omega_1=y/2-1/4$ and $\omega_2=1-y/8$; both lie in $(0,1)$. Then
$\omega_2^2-\omega_1^2=15/16-15y^2/64\in\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12]$, and $\omega_1^2$ is irrational
because $y$ is. Moreover $X_{k+1}(\omega_1)=X_k(y)$ for $k\ge2$, and
$X_{k+3}(\omega_2)=1-X_k(y)$ for all $k$, since $y$ is irrational. If
$f_N(y)<2/5$ for all large $N$, Lemma~\ref{lem:shift} gives
$\limsup f_N(\omega_1)\le9/20$ and $\limsup f_N(\omega_2)\ge11/20$,
contradicting $\textup{(TU)}_1$ for the pair $(\omega_1^2,\omega_2^2)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:nonsquare}
Let $q\ge2$ and let $A<2^{q-1}$ be odd. Then $A^2+4^q$ is not a perfect
square. Consequently, if $n\ge3$ and $A<2^{n-2}$ is odd, then $y(A/2^n)$ is
irrational. It lies in $(1/2,1)$ and has dyadic square.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
If $A^2+4^q=Z^2$, then $(Z-A)(Z+A)=2^{2q}$, so $Z-A=2^\alpha$, $Z+A=2^\beta$
with $\alpha<\beta$. As $A$ is odd, $\alpha=1$, whence $A=2^{2q-2}-1\ge
2^{q-1}$, a contradiction. For the second statement,
$y(A/2^n)=\sqrt{A^2+4^{n-1}}/2^n$; and $A/2^n<1/4$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:step}
Assume $\textup{(TU)}_1$. Let $n\ge3$, let $A<2^{n-2}$ be odd and let $B\in\mathbb{N}$. Then
there is $m\ge B$ such that $X_m(y(A/2^n))=0$ and
$f_{m-1}(y(A/2^n))\ge2/5$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:local} and Lemma~\ref{lem:nonsquare}, there is
some $M>B$ with $f_M(y(A/2^n))\ge2/5$; now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:zero}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:x}
In the construction above:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x^2$ is a Liouville number; in particular it is irrational;
\item $S_N(x)^2\le N+1$ for all $N$; in particular $f_N(x)\to0$;
\item $f_N(y(x))\ge2/5$ for infinitely many $N$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
(1) We have $0<x^2-x_k^2\le\frac34\,2^{-n_{k+1}}<(4^{n_k})^{-k}$ because
$n_{k+1}\ge2kn_k$, and $x_k^2=A_k^2/4^{n_k}$.

(2) Given $N$, let $j$ be least with $N<n_{j+1}-1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:carry},
applied at $m=n_{j+1}-1$, the numbers $x$ and $x_j$ have the same first $N$
digits, and $S_N(x_j)\le j+1$ by the second part of Lemma~\ref{lem:carry}. If
$j\ge1$, then $N\ge n_j-1\ge3\cdot4^j-1\ge(j+1)^2-1$.

(3) Let $m=n_{j+1}$. By the choice of $n_{j+1}$, $X_m(y_j)=0$ and
$f_{m-1}(y_j)\ge2/5$. Since $y(x)+y_j>1$,
\[
0\le y(x)-y_j\le x^2-x_j^2\le\tfrac34\,2^{-m},
\]
so $\lfloor2^my_j\rfloor\le\lfloor2^my(x)\rfloor\le\lfloor2^my_j\rfloor+1$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:carry}, $y(x)$ and $y_j$ have the same first $m-1$ digits,
so $f_{m-1}(y(x))\ge2/5$ for every~$j$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Assume $\textup{(TU)}_1$ and take $x$ from the construction. Put $\nu=x^2$ and
$\nu'=x^2+1/4$. Both lie in $(0,1)$, $\nu$ is irrational by
Lemma~\ref{lem:x}(1), and $\nu'-\nu=1/4$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:x}(2),
$\limsup f_N(\sqrt\nu)=0$, while $\limsup f_N(\sqrt{\nu'})\ge2/5$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:x}(3). This contradicts $\textup{(TU)}_1$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
One can replace Proposition~\ref{prop:local} by \cite[Thm.~2]{Isa06}: under
\textup{(TU)}, $y_j=\sqrt{4^{n_j-1}+A_j^2}/2^{n_j}$ is a shift of the square root of a
non-square, hence simply normal. Proposition~\ref{prop:local} avoids this and
the passage through $\{\sqrt s\}$. The gap condition $n_{j+1}\ge4(j+1)n_j+4$
is stronger than needed for (2) and (3); it is chosen so that $x^2$ is a
Liouville number.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:ms}
Let $F\in C^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $F''>0$, and let $\mu=\mu^p_{a,t}$ be a homogeneous
self-similar measure with all $p_i>0$ and without atoms. Then there are
$\sigma>0$ and $C>0$ such that
\[
|\widehat{F\mu}(u)|\le C|u|^{-\sigma}\qquad(|u|\ge1).
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:del}
Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with
$|\widehat\mu(u)|\le C|u|^{-\sigma}$ for $|u|\ge1$, where $\sigma>0$. Then
$\mu$-almost every $z$ is simply normal to base $2$, that is,
$f_N(z)\to1/2$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
In \cite[Thm.~3.1]{MS18} it is only assumed that $\mu$ is not a single
atom; we assume that $\mu$ has no atoms, which is all we need. The theorem of \cite{DEL63} is stated
for Lebesgue measure on an interval: if $\sum_NN^{-1}I(N)<\infty$ for every
$m\ne0$, where $I(N)$ is the mean square of the Weyl sum
$N^{-1}\sum_{n\le N}e(ms_n(x))$, then $s_n(x)$ is uniformly distributed
modulo~$1$ for almost all~$x$. Its proof \cite[\S2]{DEL63} uses only that the
measure is finite, so it holds for any Borel probability measure~$\mu$. For
$s_n(x)=2^nx$ one has
\[
I(N)=N^{-2}\sum_{n,n'\le N}\widehat\mu\bigl(m(2^n-2^{n'})\bigr)\ll N^{-1}
\]
under power decay, so $\mu$-almost every $z$ is normal to base~$2$, as noted in
\cite[\S1]{MS18}. We record only simple normality to base~$2$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:cantor}
\begin{enumerate}
\item The map $\pi$ is injective and $\mu$ has no atoms.
\item For every $\iota$, $X_k(\pi(\iota))=0$ unless $3\mid k$. Hence
$S_N(\pi(\iota))\le\lfloor N/3\rfloor$ for all $N$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For every $m$, $8^m\pi(\iota)=\sum_{k<m}\iota_k8^{m-1-k}+R$ with
$0\le R\le1/7$. Hence $\lfloor8^m\pi(\iota)\rfloor$ determines
$\iota_0,\dots,\iota_{m-1}$, and $\lfloor2^{3m+r}\pi(\iota)\rfloor$ is even
for $r=1,2$. Each point of $\{0,1\}^\mathbb{N}$ has product measure at most $2^{-n}$
for every~$n$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $g(\omega)=\sqrt{\omega^2/4+1/4}$. Then $g$ is smooth with
$g''=1/(16g^3)>0$. By Theorems~\ref{thm:ms} and~\ref{thm:del} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:cantor}(1), $g(\omega)$ is simply normal to base $2$ for
$\mu$-almost every $\omega$. Since $\mu$ has no atoms, also $\omega^2$ is
irrational for $\mu$-almost every $\omega$: the exceptional set is contained
in the countable set $\{\pm\sqrt q:q\in\mathbb{Q}\}$. Fix $\omega$ with both
properties. Then $0<\omega\le1/7$. Put $\nu=\omega^2/4$ and
$\nu'=\nu+1/4=g(\omega)^2$. Both lie in $(0,1)$, $\nu$ is irrational, and
$\nu'-\nu\in\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12]$. Since $X_{k+1}(\omega/2)=X_k(\omega)$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:cantor}(2) gives $f_N(\omega/2)\le1/3+2/N\le2/5$ for $N\ge30$.
Hence
\[
\limsup f_N(\sqrt\nu)\le\tfrac25<\tfrac12=\lim f_N(\sqrt{\nu'}).\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
(i) The measure $\mu$ is an affine image of the Bernoulli convolution
$\nu_{1/8}$, the distribution of $\sum_{n\ge1}\pm8^{-n}$. According to
\cite[\S1]{MS18}, Kaufman \cite{Kau84} proved $\dim_F(F\nu_a)>0$ for all
$a\in(0,1/2)$ and all $C^2$ diffeomorphisms $F$ with $F''>0$, so for this
measure Theorem~\ref{thm:ms} is already due to him; Theorem~\ref{thm:ms}
extends and quantifies his argument.

(ii) The proof shows more: \textup{(TU)}{} fails at $(\omega^2/4,\omega^2/4+1/4)$ for
$\mu$-almost every $\omega$, a set of Hausdorff dimension $1/3$. The same
argument works for the Bernoulli measure of parameter $p\ne1/2$ on the dyadic
digits. That measure gives a set of dimension close to $1$ for $p$ close to
$1/2$. It requires the strong law of large numbers in place of
Lemma~\ref{lem:cantor}(2).
<!-- end remark-4 -->
